newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Reanalysis shows 8-mth-old Australia job boom.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Reanalysis shows 8-mth-old Australia job boom.

text.p: Australia is generating about 18,000 jobs a month and has been since its labour market suddenly stepped up a gear around June, according to a reanalysis of Australian Bureau of Statistics data.

The analysis - trend estimates amended for a survey change affecting the published data - shows that the soft jobs market is not something that has recently faded out of the data, as commonly supposed.
In fact, it's ancient history, raising doubts about the need for the Reserve Bank's December cut in interest rates.

"When the bank cut interest rates last time they didn't have the benefit of the Australian Bureau of Statistics' latest thoughts on the effect of telephone interviewing," Macquarie Bank economist Andrew Ticehurst said, reviewing the corrected trend data.
"Trend employment growth is obviously stronger than was thought at the time and over coming months it should bring down the unemployment rate faster than was expected then," he said.

The bank effected a third consecutive 0.5-percentage-point rate cut on December 11, a few days before it was reported that the Australian Bureau of Statistics' shift to telephone interviewing was understating the strength of the labour market.

The new survey method is not necessarily less accurate than the old one but the bureau confirmed in mid January that the changeover was pushing down its jobs growth figures by 6,000 to 9,000 (about 0.1 percent) in each month since August.
The bureau has not, however, amended its reported data and the table below shows a Reuters calculation of trend estimates based on the seasonally adjusted data amended to remove the telephone effect.
On that basis the trend unemployment rate dropped to 8.4 percent in January from an August peak of 8.6 percent.

"Only a few weeks ago there was a solid school of economists willing to put their names to view that unemployment was going to nine percent in the first half of this year," said Bankers Trust chief economist Chris Caton, who was sure it would not happen. Trend workforce participation was 63.8 percent in
January, up from a 63.5 percent trough that appeared in May.
Most of the new jobs growth have been part-time, however.
Trend full-time jobs growth peaked at 10,500 in July and subsided to only about 500 in January. Through the same period part-time jobs growth rose from 6,000 to 17,400.
Access Economics analyst Chris Richardson said this meant the labour market was still trailing other parts of the economy.
"We will get the translation into full-timers this year," he forecast.
